checkpoint_text:
Step 1: Let \( x = (\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{5})^6 \). We need to find the greatest integer less than \( x \).

Step 2: Consider the conjugate of \( \sqrt{7} + \sqrt{5} \), which is \( \sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5} \). Note that \( 0 < \sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5} < 1 \).

Step 3: Calculate \( (\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5})^6 \). Since \( 0 < \sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5} < 1 \), it follows that \( 0 < (\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5})^6 < 1 \).

Step 4: Add the two expressions \( (\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{5})^6 \) and \( (\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5})^6 \):
\[ (\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{5})^6 + (\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5})^6 \]
This sum will be an integer because all irrational parts will cancel out.

Step 5: Expand \( (\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{5})^6 \) and \( (\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{5})^6 \) using the binomial theorem. The terms involving odd powers of \( \sqrt{7} \) and \( \sqrt{5} \) will cancel out when added together, leaving only terms with even powers.
